transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I can’t stop noticing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s in every photo, every reflection... and even when people say I look fine, it feels really obvious to me. It’s gotten to the point where I’m avoiding presentations and meeting with clients.
Can you describe how long this concern about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw has been bothering you, and has it affected your mood or caused you significant distress?

It’s been bothering me a lot. I can’t stop seeing the droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw—like in every photo or reflection. Even when people tell me I look fine, it still feels really obvious to me. It’s been very upsetting, and I’ve started avoiding presentations and meeting with clients because of it.
Do you find yourself checking your reflection, taking pictures, or doing anything repeatedly to look at or fix the area around your mouth and jaw?

Yes. Before work or if there’s a family event, I can get stuck in the bathroom for hours checking the mirror. I take pictures on my phone from different angles to see if the droop shows, and I’ll keep redoing my makeup or adjusting a scarf to try to cover it.

I also ask my husband over and over if my face looks lopsided. And then sometimes I end up scrolling through photos of other women, comparing my face to theirs, which usually just makes me feel worse.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent preoccupation with perceived facial asymmetry, repetitive checking behaviors, and significant distress and avoidance are highly indicative of Body Dysmorphic Disorder. Other candidates have been ruled out based on the absence of key features such as delusions (ruling out F22.0), primary mood episodes (ruling out F32.0-F32.9), or other specified somatic symptom disorders (ruling out F45.8).
